publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Improvement in OCD symptoms associated with serotoninergic psychedelics: a retrospective online survey

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether people with OCD symptoms who have taken psychoactive drugs report symptom change, and which drugs
span.quote: A renewed interest in the use of psychedelics for treating obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) has emerged in the last 20 years. But pre-clinical and clinical evidence remain scarce, and little is known about the factor determining the magnitude and persistence of the therapeutic effect.

span.label: which substances are reported as improving OCD symptoms, and what predicts the size and persistence of the reported effect
span.quote: In a sample of 174 participants, classic psychedelics were reported as the only substances effective at reducing OCD symptoms. In classic psychedelics users, symptoms reduction was associated with the intensity of acute effects, itself correlated to the dose.

span.label: reports that classic psychedelics alone were associated with improvement in this sample, with the reported gain tracking the intensity of acute effects and the intensity tracking dose
span.quote: In a sample of 174 participants, classic psychedelics were reported as the only substances effective at reducing OCD symptoms. In classic psychedelics users, symptoms reduction was associated with the intensity of acute effects, itself correlated to the dose.

span.label: existence
span.quote: In a sample of 174 participants, classic psychedelics were reported as the only substances effective at reducing OCD symptoms.

span.label: self-reported reduction of OCD symptoms after psychedelic use
span.quote: We therefore designed a retrospective online survey to explore, in the general population using psychoactive drugs, their impact on OCD symptoms.

span.label: retrospective-survey
span.quote: The present retrospective, online and anonymous survey aimed to evaluate, in the general population with OCD symptoms, which substances among multiple psychoactive drugs might have a therapeutic effect.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: dose raises the intensity of the acute subjective experience, and it is that intensity which drives the size of the symptom reduction
span.quote: In classic psychedelics users, symptoms reduction was associated with the intensity of acute effects, itself correlated to the dose.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: drug-induced neuroplasticity (neuronal growth and synaptogenesis) as the candidate route by which a single exposure produces long-lasting benefit
span.quote: One candidate is the neuroplastic property of psychedelics, with increased neuronal growth and synaptogenesis observed both in vivo in rodents and in vitro in different species

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: therapeutic benefit feeds back on consumption: a larger and longer-lasting improvement changes whether and how often the substance is taken again
span.quote: Finally, substance usage appeared to be tuned to the therapeutic effect.

span.label: the proposed route is dose to intensity of acute experience to therapeutic effect, with each link measured by self-report
span.quote: In a sample of 174 participants, classic psychedelics were reported as the only substances effective at reducing OCD symptoms. In classic psychedelics users, symptoms reduction was associated with the intensity of acute effects, itself correlated to the dose.

span.label: neuroplasticity is offered as the candidate for long-lasting effects, but the animal evidence is not specific to psychedelics
span.quote: One candidate is the neuroplastic property of psychedelics, with increased neuronal growth and synaptogenesis observed both in vivo in rodents and in vitro in different species 47 – 49 . In rodent, these structural modifications lasted up to a month, but were not specific to classic psychedelics since it was observed with multiple components including ketamine

span.label: DMT and mescaline may fail to appear effective because their pharmacology diverges from LSD and psilocybin despite the shared category
span.quote: Similarly, DMT and mescaline were not selected as effective for OCD symptoms. Despite being categorized as serotoninergic hallucinogens, DMT and mescaline have phenomenological and pharmacological profiles that seem to differ from LSD or psilocybin 33 . Among other differences, DMT has no affinity for the serotoninergic receptor 2C, as well as a lower hallucinogenic potency and duration of action in human 34 . Mescaline on the other side, seems to have combined psychedelic and entactogenic properties 35 and does not act on raphe neurons

span.label: later intake is predicted by how much the substance helped rather than by how pleasant it was, which the paper reads as absence of reinforcement
span.quote: Indeed, the occurrence of subsequent intakes was predicted by the magnitude of OCD symptoms improvement, with participants with stronger therapeutic effect being more likely to take the substance again. And among the participants who used the substance again, the frequency of subsequent intakes was related to the persistence of the therapeutic effect, with long-lasting (> 3 months) improvements predicting a lower frequency of intake.

span.label: Web-based recruitment introduces participant selection bias.
span.quote: In general, web-based surveys are subject to bias in participant selection.

span.label: People with pleasant experiences and positive outcomes were more likely to take part, limiting generalisability.
span.quote: Participants with a pleasant acute experience and positive outcome (i.e., improvement in OCD symptoms) were also more likely to enter the survey, limiting the generalizability of our results.

span.label: Persistence data are imprecise because the delay between drug intake and completing the survey was not recorded.
span.quote: We acknowledge that reports on persistence are not precise enough since we do not know when the intake occurred relative to the filling of the survey.

span.label: The retrospective design precludes inferring a causal link between repeat intake and the therapeutic effect.
span.quote: The causal relationship between the occurrence of subsequent intake and the therapeutic effect cannot be inferred, mainly due to the retrospective nature of our study.

span.label: Therapeutic benefit was self-assessed and therefore vulnerable to subjectivity bias.
span.quote: The self-assessment of the therapeutic effect makes it prone to subjectivity bias, but a vast majority of classic psychedelics users, in our sample, perceived an improvement in their medical conditions following the intake of the substance.

span.label: respondents were likely favourable to psychedelics and those with positive outcomes more likely to take part, which the paper says limits generalisability
span.quote: In general, web-based surveys are subject to bias in participant selection. In the context of our study, participants were likely to be favorable to the use of psychedelic drugs, which might have had an impact on their trustfulness and might have induced proselytism when completing the survey. Participants with a pleasant acute experience and positive outcome (i.e., improvement in OCD symptoms) were also more likely to enter the survey, limiting the generalizability of our results.

span.label: no causal relationship can be inferred because the design is retrospective
span.quote: The causal relationship between the occurrence of subsequent intake and the therapeutic effect cannot be inferred, mainly due to the retrospective nature of our study.

span.label: the pleasantness correlation is suspected by the authors to be a carry-over from global impression rather than a real relation
span.quote: In our survey, the magnitude of the therapeutic effect was also correlated with the pleasantness of acute effects, but we suspect a carry-over effect. Indeed, the scoring of the therapeutic effect might have been strongly influenced by the global impression of the participants on the acute subjective experience, regardless of any causal relation.

span.label: persistence data are imprecise because the time between intake and survey was never recorded
span.quote: As mentioned in the results section, the persistence data were imprecise since we did not have access to the time delay between the intake of the psychoactive drugs and the filling of the survey. This might have impacted the proportion of participants declaring short-lasting effects, with people filling out the survey shortly after the intake of the substance not being able to assess the maintenance of the therapeutic effect in the long term.

span.label: mindset and setting were assessed coarsely and their null effect is not strong evidence of no effect
span.quote: We also included as factors in the model the mindset and context of the intake and did not observe any impact of it. However, we acknowledge that the assessment of these parameters was rather coarse in our study, and it seems reasonable to think that the context of the intake at least, might impact the pleasantness of the experience.

span.label: the ketamine comparison is not usable because recreational use differs from clinical use in enantiomer, dose and route
span.quote: Previous results on the use of ketamine in OCD are mixed 32 , but our results are difficult to compare since recreational use differs from therapeutic guidelines in terms of enantiomer, dose and mode of administration.

span.label: the paper states the results should not be generalised until randomised trials confirm them
span.quote: All limitations related to online surveys should be kept in mind, and these results should not be generalized to the entire OCD population until the outcome of randomized controlled clinical trials confirms our observations.

span.label: the anonymous online survey, adopted because the substances are illegal and cannot easily be studied otherwise
span.quote: Since psychedelics have been classified under Schedule I in the 1971 conventions of the United Nations 21 and remain illegal in many countries, observational studies such as anonymous online surveys have been used to assess the use, misuse and potential therapeutic properties of psychedelics

span.label: the OCI-r severity scale, used to screen respondents who had no clinical diagnosis
span.quote: We then selected our population of interest based on OCD symptoms and kept for analyses the data from participants who had either a diagnosis of OCD performed by a health professional (n = 9), or an OCI-r score superior to 18 (n = 62) 29 or both (n = 103). The rationale was to include participants who had not been screened by a psychiatrist or a psychologist (participants without diagnosis but OCI-r > 18), and participants in remission when filling out the survey (participants with a diagnosis but OCI-r < 18). Using these criteria, we identified 174 participants (76% from the English survey).

span.label: OCD here is EITHER a professional diagnosis OR a self-report with OCI-r above 18 - one of the two entry routes involves no clinician at all
span.quote: We then selected our population of interest based on OCD symptoms and kept for analyses the data from participants who had either a diagnosis of OCD performed by a health professional (n = 9), or an OCI-r score superior to 18 (n = 62) 29 or both (n = 103). The rationale was to include participants who had not been screened by a psychiatrist or a psychologist (participants without diagnosis but OCI-r > 18), and participants in remission when filling out the survey (participants with a diagnosis but OCI-r < 18). Using these criteria, we identified 174 participants (76% from the English survey).

span.label: the analysed effect sample is conditioned on the dependent variable: respondents answering No to having experienced any change were sent straight to the end of the survey
span.quote: The first question was “ Have you experienced a change in your OCD as a result of taking a psychedelic? ” Participants answering No were redirected toward the end of the survey, whereas participants answering Yes had to select the substance that induced the strongest changes in OCD symptoms, among the list presented in part III.

span.label: dose is a self-recalled quantity converted by a fixed factor - grams of dried mushroom multiplied by 0.0063 to give milligrams of psilocybin - so it carries both recall error and a species assumption
span.quote: For psilocybin mushrooms, most of the doses were expressed as grams of dried mushrooms, which we converted into milligrams of psilocybin by multiplying by a 0.0063 factor (appropriate for Psilocybe cubensis type of mushrooms according to 30 ). Following this transformation, the mean(SD) dose of psilocybin was 20.30 (16.74)mg, ranging from 1 to 88 and the mean(SD) dose of LSD was 131.56 (69.85)μg, ranging from 10 to 250 (Fig. 3 B).

span.label: improvement is a single retrospective cursor position from -100 to +100, not a repeated clinical measure, and the OCI-r was collected only at survey time
span.quote: Each item was scored by moving a cursor on a 100-point scale (2-point step) starting at midpoint (0: no change ) and ranging from -100 ( Worsening ) to + 100 ( Improvement ).

span.label: classic psychedelics is a category that behaves inhomogeneously here - LSD and psilocybin drive the result while DMT and mescaline do not
span.quote: Similarly, DMT and mescaline were not selected as effective for OCD symptoms. Despite being categorized as serotoninergic hallucinogens, DMT and mescaline have phenomenological and pharmacological profiles that seem to differ from LSD or psilocybin 33 . Among other differences, DMT has no affinity for the serotoninergic receptor 2C, as well as a lower hallucinogenic potency and duration of action in human 34 . Mescaline on the other side, seems to have combined psychedelic and entactogenic properties 35 and does not act on raphe neurons

span.label: extends → case reports and a nine-patient open-label psilocybin trial whose follow-up ran only 24 hours
span.quote: Evidence remains scarce with the most substantial study being an open-label trial, in which 9 patients with moderate to severe OCD were exposed to various doses of psilocybin ranging from low sub-hallucinogenic to high hallucinogenic ones 13 . This trial suggested that psilocybin might be efficient in decreasing OCD symptoms, but the follow-up was limited to 24 h and long-term effects were not assessed.

span.label: contradicts → a previous survey finding no relationship between pleasantness of acute effects and enduring well-being in healthy subjects
span.quote: Additionally, previous survey has reported, in healthy subjects, the lack of relationship between the pleasantness of acute effects and the enduring well-being induced by psilocybin

span.label: qualifies → its own pleasantness result, by proposing a carry-over artefact as the likely explanation
span.quote: In our survey, the magnitude of the therapeutic effect was also correlated with the pleasantness of acute effects, but we suspect a carry-over effect. Indeed, the scoring of the therapeutic effect might have been strongly influenced by the global impression of the participants on the acute subjective experience, regardless of any causal relation.

span.label: distinguishes-from → clinical ketamine studies, on enantiomer, dose and route
span.quote: Previous results on the use of ketamine in OCD are mixed 32 , but our results are difficult to compare since recreational use differs from therapeutic guidelines in terms of enantiomer, dose and mode of administration.

span.label: supports → reports of psychedelic effects persisting for weeks to months in other conditions
span.quote: Regarding the persistence of the therapeutic effect, over 30% of participants reported effects lasting for more than three months. However, no significant predictor was detected that could explain the variability of reports.

span.label: RETRACTED (REVERSED) · classic psychedelics —part-of→ psilocybin
span.quote: As shown in Table 3 , the most used substance categories among our OCD population were classic psychedelics (84%), entactogens (72%) and ketamine (49%); whereas NPS, delirogens and ibogaine were used by 22%, 16% and 2% of the participants, respectively.

span.label: RETRACTED (THE SPAN MAKES DMT A MEMBER OF THE CLASS THE EDGE EXCLUDES IT FROM) · DMT —distinct-from→ classic psychedelics
span.quote: Similarly, DMT and mescaline were not selected as effective for OCD symptoms. Despite being categorized as serotoninergic hallucinogens, DMT and mescaline have phenomenological and pharmacological profiles that seem to differ from LSD or psilocybin 33 . Among other differences, DMT has no affinity for the serotoninergic receptor 2C, as well as a lower hallucinogenic potency and duration of action in human 34 . Mescaline on the other side, seems to have combined psychedelic and entactogenic properties 35 and does not act on raphe neurons

span.label: acute effects —causes→ OCD
span.quote: In a sample of 174 participants, classic psychedelics were reported as the only substances effective at reducing OCD symptoms. In classic psychedelics users, symptoms reduction was associated with the intensity of acute effects, itself correlated to the dose.

span.label: pleasantness —distinct-from→ acute effects
span.quote: In our survey, the magnitude of the therapeutic effect was also correlated with the pleasantness of acute effects, but we suspect a carry-over effect. Indeed, the scoring of the therapeutic effect might have been strongly influenced by the global impression of the participants on the acute subjective experience, regardless of any causal relation.

span.label: OCI-r —operationalised-as→ OCD
span.quote: We then selected our population of interest based on OCD symptoms and kept for analyses the data from participants who had either a diagnosis of OCD performed by a health professional (n = 9), or an OCI-r score superior to 18 (n = 62) 29 or both (n = 103). The rationale was to include participants who had not been screened by a psychiatrist or a psychologist (participants without diagnosis but OCI-r > 18), and participants in remission when filling out the survey (participants with a diagnosis but OCI-r < 18). Using these criteria, we identified 174 participants (76% from the English survey).

span.label: recall bias —causes→ acute effects
span.quote: The evaluation of acute effects is intrinsically subjective, and the retrospective design of the study could have affected the scorings due to recall bias. However, the observation of an already described and therefore expected link between the intensity of acute effects and the dose 38 , suggests that their evaluations were somewhat trustful.

span.label: ketamine —contrasted-with→ classic psychedelics
span.quote: Classic psychedelics were selected as the most impacting substances by 66% of the participants who declared using them. This proportion was 15% for entactogens, 7% for ketamine, 7% for delirogens and 0% for NPS. A χ 2 test applied to categories with sufficient number of observations (n > 5) revealed that the proportion of participants declaring a substance category as the most impacting one varied according to the substance category (χ 2 (2) = 113.5, P < 0.001; Fig. 2 A), with a significant difference in proportion between classic psychedelics and entactogens (P < 0.001) and between classic psychedelics and ketamine (P < 0.001) but no difference between entactogens and ketamine (P = 0.11).

span.label: entactogens —contrasted-with→ classic psychedelics
span.quote: When looking at the changes in OCD symptoms induced by the intake of each substance, we observed that mean changes were positive and significant for classic psychedelics (mean(SE) = + 42.62 (3.79), t(95) = 11.24, P < 0.001) but not for entactogens (mean(SE) = + 4.73 (10.69), t(18) = 0.44, P = 0.66) or ketamine (mean(SE) = + 8.00 (13.65), t(5) = 0.59, P = 0.58; Fig. 1 C).

span.label: persistence —operationalised-as→ OCD
span.quote: As mentioned in the results section, the persistence data were imprecise since we did not have access to the time delay between the intake of the psychoactive drugs and the filling of the survey. This might have impacted the proportion of participants declaring short-lasting effects, with people filling out the survey shortly after the intake of the substance not being able to assess the maintenance of the therapeutic effect in the long term.

span.label: SSRIs —operationalised-as→ OCD
span.quote: Evidence remains scarce with the most substantial study being an open-label trial, in which 9 patients with moderate to severe OCD were exposed to various doses of psilocybin ranging from low sub-hallucinogenic to high hallucinogenic ones 13 . This trial suggested that psilocybin might be efficient in decreasing OCD symptoms, but the follow-up was limited to 24 h and long-term effects were not assessed.

span.label: neuroplastic —causes→ persistence
span.quote: One candidate is the neuroplastic property of psychedelics, with increased neuronal growth and synaptogenesis observed both in vivo in rodents and in vitro in different species 47 – 49 . In rodent, these structural modifications lasted up to a month, but were not specific to classic psychedelics since it was observed with multiple components including ketamine

span.label: chi-squared
span.quote: A chi-squared (χ 2 ) test was used to test if the proportion of users declaring a given substance as the most impacting one varied according to the substance, and one-sample Student’s t-tests were used to evaluate if the magnitudes of the changes induced by the different substances were significantly different from 0.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: A chi-squared (χ 2 ) test was used to test if the proportion of users declaring a given substance as the most impacting one varied according to the substance, and one-sample Student’s t-tests were used to evaluate if the magnitudes of the changes induced by the different substances were significantly different from 0.

span.label: regression
span.quote: To evaluate which factor might predict the magnitude of the changes in OCD symptoms, a linear regression was used that included 6 independent variables:

span.label: ordinal regression
span.quote: To evaluate which variables might predict the persistence of the changes in OCD symptoms, an ordinal regression was used with 5 regressors:

span.label: logistic regression
span.quote: was regressed out using a logistic regression with 6 regressors:

span.label: multiple-comparison correction
span.quote: the associated p-values were corrected for multiple comparison using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.

span.label: variance inflation factor
span.quote: Additionally, multicollinearity between independent variables has been assessed for all regressions using the generalized variance inflation factor (GVIF).

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: the line and ribbon represent the estimated regression line and its 95% confidence interval.

span.label: mean
span.quote: we used the within-participant mean of the ratings on the different subscales

span.label: standard error
span.quote: black dots and bars represent the means and standard errors across participant, respectively.

span.label: χ 2 test
span.quote: Classic psychedelics were selected as the most impacting substances by 66% of the participants who declared using them. This proportion was 15% for entactogens, 7% for ketamine, 7% for delirogens and 0% for NPS. A χ 2 test applied to categories with sufficient number of observations (n > 5) revealed that the proportion of participants declaring a substance category as the most impacting one varied according to the substance category (χ 2 (2) = 113.5, P < 0.001; Fig. 2 A), with a significant difference in proportion between classic psychedelics and entactogens (P < 0.001) and between classic psychedelics and ketamine (P < 0.001) but no difference between entactogens and ketamine (P = 0.11).

span.label: one-sample t-tests
span.quote: When looking at the changes in OCD symptoms induced by the intake of each substance, we observed that mean changes were positive and significant for classic psychedelics (mean(SE) = + 42.62 (3.79), t(95) = 11.24, P < 0.001) but not for entactogens (mean(SE) = + 4.73 (10.69), t(18) = 0.44, P = 0.66) or ketamine (mean(SE) = + 8.00 (13.65), t(5) = 0.59, P = 0.58; Fig. 1 C).

span.label: Classic psychedelics were the only substance category that produced a significant improvement in OCD symptoms, both by proportion of users reporting change and by direction of that change.
span.quote: Classic psychedelics appeared as the only substance category inducing a significant improvement in OCD symptoms, both in terms of the proportion of users declaring a change and the direction of the change.

span.label: The size of the OCD improvement was predicted by how intense and how pleasant the acute drug experience was, and not by the user's expectations or the context of the intake.
span.quote: This analysis shows that the improvement in OCD symptoms was not associated with the mindset or context of intake but was larger for more intense and more pleasant acute effects.

span.label: Because reported intensity of acute effects tracked the reported dose, intensity could be used as a stand-in for dose across the whole sample.
span.quote: This analysis shows that in our dataset, the intensity of acute effects can be used as a proxy for the dose, with increasing doses leading to more intense experiences.

span.label: No measured variable predicted how long the OCD improvement lasted.
span.quote: Results showed that none of the regressors significantly predicted the persistence of the improvement

span.label: Whether and how often people took the substance again was governed by the size and duration of the symptom improvement rather than by how intense or pleasant the trip had been.
span.quote: This last analysis shows that in our dataset, the occurrence and frequency of subsequent intakes were not related to the intensity or pleasantness of acute effects but to the improvement in OCD symptoms and its persistence.

span.label: A minority of respondents reported that their OCD symptoms got worse rather than better.
span.quote: We should mention that 10% of participants reported a worsening of OCD symptoms.

span.label: classic psychedelics were chosen as the most impacting substance by 66% of those who had used them
span.quote: Classic psychedelics were selected as the most impacting substances by 66% of the participants who declared using them. This proportion was 15% for entactogens, 7% for ketamine, 7% for delirogens and 0% for NPS. A χ 2 test applied to categories with sufficient number of observations (n > 5) revealed that the proportion of participants declaring a substance category as the most impacting one varied according to the substance category (χ 2 (2) = 113.5, P < 0.001; Fig. 2 A), with a significant difference in proportion between classic psychedelics and entactogens (P < 0.001) and between classic psychedelics and ketamine (P < 0.001) but no difference between entactogens and ketamine (P = 0.11).

span.label: mean reported change was positive and significant for classic psychedelics but not for entactogens or ketamine
span.quote: When looking at the changes in OCD symptoms induced by the intake of each substance, we observed that mean changes were positive and significant for classic psychedelics (mean(SE) = + 42.62 (3.79), t(95) = 11.24, P < 0.001) but not for entactogens (mean(SE) = + 4.73 (10.69), t(18) = 0.44, P = 0.66) or ketamine (mean(SE) = + 8.00 (13.65), t(5) = 0.59, P = 0.58; Fig. 1 C).

span.label: psilocybin and LSD each showed a significant mean improvement and did not differ from one another
span.quote: Within the classic psychedelics category, mean changes were positive and significant for both psilocybin mushrooms (mean(SE) = + 44.22 (4.66), t(55) = 9.49, P < 0.001) and LSD (mean(SE) = + 40.23 (5.95), t(33) = 6.76, P < 0.001; Fig. 1 D).

span.label: over 30% reported effects lasting more than three months, with no predictor of that variability found
span.quote: Regarding the persistence of the therapeutic effect, over 30% of participants reported effects lasting for more than three months. However, no significant predictor was detected that could explain the variability of reports.

span.label: subsequent intake was predicted by how much the substance helped, and its frequency by how long the help lasted
span.quote: Indeed, the occurrence of subsequent intakes was predicted by the magnitude of OCD symptoms improvement, with participants with stronger therapeutic effect being more likely to take the substance again. And among the participants who used the substance again, the frequency of subsequent intakes was related to the persistence of the therapeutic effect, with long-lasting (> 3 months) improvements predicting a lower frequency of intake.

span.label: 10% of participants reported a worsening of OCD symptoms
span.quote: We should mention that 10% of participants reported a worsening of OCD symptoms. Whether similar proportion are observed in well-controlled clinical trials is an important matter, which would call for an evaluation of risk factors.

span.label: no apparent case of substance abuse was reported, consistent with psychedelics lacking reinforcing properties
span.quote: We did not observe any apparent case of substance abuse from participants’ reports, with no or very moderate intake repetition in most of them. This is coherent with the literature reporting no reinforcing properties of classic psychedelics, neither in humans nor in animals

span.label: 82% of classic psychedelic users had also used at least one other substance category
span.quote: When looking at combinations of substances, we observed that 82% of classic psychedelics users had also used at least one other substance category. This proportion was 92% for entactogens users, 95% for ketamine users, 97% for NPS users and 100% for delirogens and ibogaine users.

span.label: the authors read that polydrug use as support for the comparison, since respondents could compare substances
span.quote: The fact that many participants used multiple substances brings additional credits to their choice, since they were likely able to compare between substances.

span.label: CALIBRATION CHECK: the known dose-to-intensity relation was reproduced, which the paper uses as evidence that the self-ratings were trustworthy
span.quote: The evaluation of acute effects is intrinsically subjective, and the retrospective design of the study could have affected the scorings due to recall bias. However, the observation of an already described and therefore expected link between the intensity of acute effects and the dose 38 , suggests that their evaluations were somewhat trustful.

span.label: VALIDITY CHECK: therapy and medication use, sex ratio and comorbidity rates matched published OCD epidemiology
span.quote: Still, we attempted to objectively evaluate symptom severity using the OCI-r. The answers provided by our participants with OCD symptoms were also coherent with the literature on OCD management, with the most used therapy and medications in our sample being cognitive-behavioral therapy and antidepressant, which are the two recommended first-line therapeutic approaches for OCD 3 . Also, the ratio between male and female as well as the rate of comorbidities were very similar in our sample when compared to epidemiological studies on OCD

span.label: SAMPLE CONDITIONED ON THE OUTCOME: respondents reporting no change were routed straight to the end of the survey
span.quote: The first question was “ Have you experienced a change in your OCD as a result of taking a psychedelic? ” Participants answering No were redirected toward the end of the survey, whereas participants answering Yes had to select the substance that induced the strongest changes in OCD symptoms, among the list presented in part III.

span.label: SELECTION BIAS STATED: respondents were likely favourable to psychedelics and those with good outcomes more likely to take part
span.quote: In general, web-based surveys are subject to bias in participant selection. In the context of our study, participants were likely to be favorable to the use of psychedelic drugs, which might have had an impact on their trustfulness and might have induced proselytism when completing the survey. Participants with a pleasant acute experience and positive outcome (i.e., improvement in OCD symptoms) were also more likely to enter the survey, limiting the generalizability of our results.

span.label: SELF-DISOWNED RESULT: the pleasantness correlation is attributed by the authors to a probable carry-over effect
span.quote: In our survey, the magnitude of the therapeutic effect was also correlated with the pleasantness of acute effects, but we suspect a carry-over effect. Indeed, the scoring of the therapeutic effect might have been strongly influenced by the global impression of the participants on the acute subjective experience, regardless of any causal relation.

span.label: NOT TO BE GENERALISED: the paper states its results should not be extended to the OCD population until randomised trials confirm them
span.quote: All limitations related to online surveys should be kept in mind, and these results should not be generalized to the entire OCD population until the outcome of randomized controlled clinical trials confirms our observations.

span.label: classic psychedelics / serotoninergic hallucinogens
span.quote: Classic psychedelics are also called serotoninergic hallucinogens since these substances are thought to exert their effects by a partial agonist action on 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) 2A receptors.

span.label: mindset and setting
span.quote: as well as the mindset (i.e., the expectations or state of mind when taking the substance) and setting (i.e., the context of the intake)

span.label: substance categories (5-category grouping scheme)
span.quote: First, substances were grouped into 5 substance categories based on their chemical properties and subjective effects as follows:

span.label: classic psychedelics
span.quote: A renewed interest in the use of psychedelics for treating obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) has emerged in the last 20 years. But pre-clinical and clinical evidence remain scarce, and little is known about the factor determining the magnitude and persistence of the therapeutic effect.

span.label: OCI-r
span.quote: We then selected our population of interest based on OCD symptoms and kept for analyses the data from participants who had either a diagnosis of OCD performed by a health professional (n = 9), or an OCI-r score superior to 18 (n = 62) 29 or both (n = 103). The rationale was to include participants who had not been screened by a psychiatrist or a psychologist (participants without diagnosis but OCI-r > 18), and participants in remission when filling out the survey (participants with a diagnosis but OCI-r < 18). Using these criteria, we identified 174 participants (76% from the English survey).

span.label: pleasantness
span.quote: Each item was scored by moving a cursor on a 100-point scale (2-point step) starting at midpoint (0: no change ) and ranging from -100 ( Worsening ) to + 100 ( Improvement ).

span.label: substance (LSD vs psilocybin mushrooms)

span.term: persistence of the change in OCD symptoms
span.quote: The persistence of these changes was also examined with participants choosing between a few hours, less than a day, one to three days, three days to a week, between a week and a month, one to three months, more than three months, permanently .

span.label: acute effects
span.quote: In a sample of 174 participants, classic psychedelics were reported as the only substances effective at reducing OCD symptoms. In classic psychedelics users, symptoms reduction was associated with the intensity of acute effects, itself correlated to the dose.

span.label: persistence
span.quote: Regarding the persistence of the therapeutic effect, over 30% of participants reported effects lasting for more than three months. However, no significant predictor was detected that could explain the variability of reports.

span.label: 174 — respondents analysed, from 227 who entered the survey
span.quote: We then selected our population of interest based on OCD symptoms and kept for analyses the data from participants who had either a diagnosis of OCD performed by a health professional (n = 9), or an OCI-r score superior to 18 (n = 62) 29 or both (n = 103). The rationale was to include participants who had not been screened by a psychiatrist or a psychologist (participants without diagnosis but OCI-r > 18), and participants in remission when filling out the survey (participants with a diagnosis but OCI-r < 18). Using these criteria, we identified 174 participants (76% from the English survey).

span.label: 66% — of classic psychedelic users who named them the most impacting substance
span.quote: Classic psychedelics were selected as the most impacting substances by 66% of the participants who declared using them. This proportion was 15% for entactogens, 7% for ketamine, 7% for delirogens and 0% for NPS. A χ 2 test applied to categories with sufficient number of observations (n > 5) revealed that the proportion of participants declaring a substance category as the most impacting one varied according to the substance category (χ 2 (2) = 113.5, P < 0.001; Fig. 2 A), with a significant difference in proportion between classic psychedelics and entactogens (P < 0.001) and between classic psychedelics and ketamine (P < 0.001) but no difference between entactogens and ketamine (P = 0.11).

span.label: +42.62 — mean reported change for classic psychedelics on a scale from -100 to +100
span.quote: When looking at the changes in OCD symptoms induced by the intake of each substance, we observed that mean changes were positive and significant for classic psychedelics (mean(SE) = + 42.62 (3.79), t(95) = 11.24, P < 0.001) but not for entactogens (mean(SE) = + 4.73 (10.69), t(18) = 0.44, P = 0.66) or ketamine (mean(SE) = + 8.00 (13.65), t(5) = 0.59, P = 0.58; Fig. 1 C).

span.label: 10% — participants reporting a worsening of symptoms
span.quote: We should mention that 10% of participants reported a worsening of OCD symptoms. Whether similar proportion are observed in well-controlled clinical trials is an important matter, which would call for an evaluation of risk factors.

span.label: over 30% — reporting benefit lasting more than three months
span.quote: Regarding the persistence of the therapeutic effect, over 30% of participants reported effects lasting for more than three months. However, no significant predictor was detected that could explain the variability of reports.

span.label: 0.0063 — factor converting grams of dried mushroom to milligrams of psilocybin, assuming Psilocybe cubensis
span.quote: For psilocybin mushrooms, most of the doses were expressed as grams of dried mushrooms, which we converted into milligrams of psilocybin by multiplying by a 0.0063 factor (appropriate for Psilocybe cubensis type of mushrooms according to 30 ). Following this transformation, the mean(SD) dose of psilocybin was 20.30 (16.74)mg, ranging from 1 to 88 and the mean(SD) dose of LSD was 131.56 (69.85)μg, ranging from 10 to 250 (Fig. 3 B).

span.label: 67% — respondents who claimed to know the dose they took, of whom 8% gave impossible values
span.quote: When asked if they knew the substance dose they had taken, 67% of the participants answered positively (Fig. 3 A). Based on the provided dosage and associated unit, 8% of them were discarded due to missing or absurd information (e.g., participants declaring the intake of 4g of LSD).

span.label: 30-40% — OCD patients who do not respond at all to first-line SSRI treatment
span.quote: Evidence remains scarce with the most substantial study being an open-label trial, in which 9 patients with moderate to severe OCD were exposed to various doses of psilocybin ranging from low sub-hallucinogenic to high hallucinogenic ones 13 . This trial suggested that psilocybin might be efficient in decreasing OCD symptoms, but the follow-up was limited to 24 h and long-term effects were not assessed.
